summary: Describes a family of tests receiving mail servers can use to check whether an email address was used with the permission of the owner of the domain. It was meant to fight spoofed addresses. It is now historic.

eli5.summary: Mail can have a fake return address. Sender ID let the receiver check whether the claimed sender's domain really allowed this mail server to send it.

questions: how to stop spoofed email addresses
how does sender id prevent email spoofing
what are the security limitations of sender id
subtitle: Check email addresses against DNS records to verify the sender's domain approved the SMTP connection.

tldr.problem: Most spam and phishing emails use forged sender addresses from domains whose owners never authorized them, making spoofed mail indistinguishable from legitimate mail.
tldr.mechanism: Sender ID adds DNS record scopes and decision logic to the SPF framework, so a receiving mail server can verify whether the SMTP client is authorized to send from the claimed sender's domain.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is Historic; DKIM and related mechanisms proved more robust and are now preferred for email authentication.

facts.label: Defined scopes
facts.value: mfrom (MAIL FROM) and pra (Purported Responsible Address)

facts.label: Result codes
facts.value: 7 (Pass, Fail, SoftFail, Neutral, None, TempError, PermError)

today: RFC 4406 is Historic. While Sender ID successfully prevented some spoofing, it did not achieve widespread adoption as the preferred email authentication method. DKIM (RFC 6376) and later SPF (RFC 7208) became more widely deployed because they provide better security properties and handle complex mail scenarios better. Sender ID's limitations—particularly the difficulty of handling forwarding and the DNS dependency—made it less attractive than DKIM's cryptographic approach.

sections.title: Email Spoofing and Verification
sections.content:
Today, the vast majority of unwanted email uses forged sender addresses. A spammer might send a message that claims to be from ceo@company.com without permission, because SMTP has no built-in way to verify that the sending mail server is authorized to do so. Phishing emails and virus-laden spam rely on this spoofing to deceive users.

Sender ID defines tests that receiving mail servers can perform to check whether a sender's domain authorized the SMTP client to send mail from that domain. Unlike some authentication schemes that protect message content, Sender ID focuses only on verifying the domain of the sender—not the local part of the address. A domain owner can declare which mail servers are authorized to send from their domain by publishing records in DNS.
sections.eli5: Spam uses fake return addresses. Sender ID lets a receiver call the company whose name is on the mail and ask, "Did you send this?"

sections.title: SPF Records and Scope
sections.content:
Domains declare authorized outbound mail servers by publishing Sender Policy Framework (SPF) records in DNS. RFC 4408 defined the v=spf1 format. Sender ID extends this with spf2.0 records that explicitly declare the scope of the record:

spf2.0/mfrom,pra +mx +ip4:192.168.0.100 -all

This record states that mail servers at the specified IPs or discovered via MX records are authorized for both the MAIL FROM check (mfrom) and the Purported Responsible Address check (pra). The two checks authenticate different addresses: MAIL FROM validates the bounce address (for DSN delivery), while PRA validates the address that appears to have most recently injected the message into the mail system (the From header in simple cases, or Resent-From in forwarded messages).

A receiving server looks up the SPF record for the sender's domain. If multiple records exist, it prefers spf2.0 records with the matching scope, falling back to v=spf1 if no spf2.0 record exists for the desired scope.
sections.eli5: A company puts in DNS: "These mail servers can send from our domain for these kinds of checks." The receiver looks it up and sees if the sender's server is on the list.

sections.title: The Verification Decision Process
sections.content:
When a receiving SMTP server processes an incoming email, it performs these steps:

1. Extract the address to verify. For PRA checks, use the Purported Responsible Address (from Resent-From, Sender, or From headers). For MAIL FROM checks, use the SMTP MAIL command address.

2. Extract the domain part of that address.

3. Call the SPF check_host() function with: the scope (pra or mfrom), the SMTP client's IP address, the domain, and the address.

The function returns one of seven results: Pass (authorized), Fail (not authorized), SoftFail (probably not authorized but server should still accept), Neutral (no opinion), None (no record found), TempError (DNS problem), or PermError (syntax error in record). Receiving servers decide what to do with each result; the spec does not mandate rejection.
sections.eli5: The receiver extracts the sender's domain, looks up the company's DNS record, calls the SPF checker, and gets an answer: yes, no, maybe, or problem.

sections.title: Security Limitations and Attacks
sections.content:
Sender ID has several known limitations:

DNS attacks: The mechanism depends entirely on DNS. An attacker who can forge DNS responses can make unauthorized servers appear authorized. DNSSEC can mitigate this.

TCP spoofing: An attacker with raw packet access can forge SMTP source addresses. This is largely mitigated by IP address filtering at network boundaries.

Forged headers: A message with a real Resent-From header but forged From header will pass PRA checks. MUAs must display the verified address to alert users.

Address hijacking: An attacker who can manipulate IP routing (e.g., via BGP hijacking) can intercept and send mail from supposedly authorized IPs.

Malicious DNS attacks on third parties: An attacker can send a spoofed message to a victim's address, causing the victim to receive error messages that reflect the attacker's content.

The spec notes that these limitations do not make Sender ID useless—it does prevent naive spoofing—but it is not a complete solution to email forgery.
sections.eli5: A clever attacker can still spoof email by faking DNS records, forging IP addresses, or manipulating mail headers. Sender ID stops easy spoofing but not determined attacks.

sections.title: Implementation and Interoperability
sections.content:
Different email infrastructure roles have different responsibilities:

Simple e-mailers: Should publish SPF records so their mail passes checks. Most should use v=spf1 format for backward compatibility with older SPF implementations.

E-mail forwarders: Must add appropriate headers (Resent-From for PRA compliance) and rewrite the MAIL FROM address to one under their control for MAIL FROM compliance, forwarding bounces to the original sender.

Mailing list servers: Must add Resent-From headers and rewrite MAIL FROM addresses similarly.

Third-party mailers: Should use a Sender header (not From) and rewrite MAIL FROM to a controlled address.

MUAs: Should display the verified address when it differs from the From header, alerting users to potential header forgery.
sections.eli5: Different mail services need different setups. Forwarders must add headers. Lists must rewrite addresses. Mail readers should show which address actually passed the check.

left.title: MAIL FROM (mfrom)
left.desc: Verifies the bounce address (SMTP MAIL command). Used by mail relays and bounces.

right.title: Purported Responsible Address (pra)
right.desc: Verifies the most recent sender in headers (Resent-From or From). Used by mail readers.
